  "content": "Keeping experiment records helps engineers because it turns a one-time observation into a reliable source of knowledge that can be reviewed, trusted, and reused. When an engineer writes down what was tested, how it was tested, what materials and settings were used, and what results were observed, the work becomes reproducible. This matters because an experiment that cannot be repeated cannot be fully verified, and engineering decisions often depend on confirming that a result is real rather than accidental.\n\nRecords also help engineers detect and correct mistakes. By comparing planned steps with what actually happened, they can spot deviations, instrument errors, or missing measurements before those problems lead to faulty conclusions. Clear records make it easier to separate what was measured from what was assumed, which reduces the risk of overconfidence in incomplete data.\n\nIn addition, experiment records support learning over time. Engineers often return to earlier work when a design fails, a test gives unexpected results, or a new project resembles an old one. Good records preserve the reasoning behind choices, not just the final numbers, so future engineers can understand why a particular approach was taken and whether it should be repeated or avoided.\n\nRecords also improve communication and accountability.
